content: I want to build an app to save and manage bookmarks.

Great — let's start by understanding what you really want out of this, before anything about screens or technology.

A bookmark app can mean very different things depending on the itch it's scratching. So, first the "why":

**When this bookmark app is finished and working well, what would be different from how you handle things today?** What's frustrating or missing right now that made you want to build this?

For example — are you drowning in browser bookmarks you can never find again? Saving links across many devices and losing track? Collecting articles/videos to read later? Sharing collections with other people? Something else entirely?

Just tell me in your own words what's going on today and what you picture being better. I'll take it from there.

Honestly, it's the browser bookmarks mess. I've got hundreds of them piled up in folders, and when I actually need one I can never find it again. The folders made sense the day I made them and now they don't.

What I really picture is one place where I dump every link worth keeping and can actually get it back later. A couple of things that frustrate me today:

- I search for a link and can't find it because I don't remember the exact title — I just remember it was "that article about Rome." So searching needs to look inside the description and my own notes too, not just the title.
- I want to slap a few labels on things instead of forcing each link into one folder. Like a recipe could be "cooking" and "italian" at the same time.
- A big pile of stuff is "I'll read this later" — articles and videos I save with every intention of getting to. Those get lost worst of all. I'd want to flag those and see just that list, then tick them off once I've read them.
- And this drives me nuts: half my old bookmarks now go to dead pages. The link rots or the site takes the article down. So whatever I save, I'd love it to keep a copy of what the page actually said, so it's not gone forever.

Basically: save fast, find it later, and don't lose it. Does that give you enough to start?

That's a really clear picture — thank you. Let me play it back to make sure I've got the direction right.

**What you want, in essence:** one place where you can dump any link worth keeping, fast, and reliably get it back later — replacing the browser-bookmark folder mess that's become impossible to search.

And underneath that, four specific frustrations you want gone:

1. **Find by memory, not exact title** — when you search, it should look inside your descriptions and notes too, so "that article about Rome" actually surfaces it.
2. **Labels, not folders** — put several labels on one link (a recipe is both "cooking" and "italian") instead of trapping it in a single folder.
3. **A "read later" pile you can actually work through** — flag things you intend to read/watch, see just that list, and tick them off once done.
4. **Survive link rot** — keep a copy of what the page said, so even if the original dies or gets taken down, your saved version isn't lost.

Your one-line summary: **save fast, find it later, and don't lose it.**

Two quick things before we dig in:

- **Is that the right direction overall?** Anything I've overstated, understated, or missed?
- **One scope check:** of those four, keeping a copy of the page (#4) is the most ambitious. Is that a must-have for this to feel worth building — or is it more of a "would be great eventually," where the real heart is #1–3 (fast save + strong search + labels + read-later)?

You've got it exactly right — that playback is spot on, nothing overstated. The one-liner "save fast, find it later, don't lose it" is really how I think about it.

On your scope question about keeping a copy of the page — I don't want to wave that away. "Don't lose it" is a third of the whole point for me, and it's the part no browser has ever done for me. So I'd call it a must-have, not a someday. That said, I'm not precious about *how* — if the honest sequencing is to nail fast-save, search, labels, and read-later first and then add the saved copy, I can live with that order. I just don't want it quietly dropped off the list. As long as it's genuinely on the roadmap, I'm happy.

One thing that came to mind while reading your list — part of why my browser bookmarks are such a swamp is that I've saved the same page three or four times over the years and ended up with duplicates. So when I go to save a link I've already got, I wouldn't want a second copy created. I'd expect it to just recognize "you already have this one" and take me to the one I've got so I can tweak it. That'd save me from the mess repeating itself.

Otherwise, yes — this is the right direction. Let's dig in.

**Saving (fast, the way you insisted)**
- Paste a link, hit Save, done — it auto-fills the page's real title, a one-line summary of what it's about, and the site's icon. No typing.

**Finding (the rescue)**

**Organizing**
- **Labels**, many per link, with an adder that nudges you to reuse ones you have (no "cooking"/"Cooking" twins); a Labels bar to jump to a topic.
- **Read-later pile:** flag things, see just that list with a live count, tick them off when read (they stay saved).

**Don't-lose-it**
- An automatic saved copy of every page, readable anytime; dead links fall back to your copy with a clear notice (no "are you sure" gate).
- **PDFs kept as the real file**, not mangled text.
- **Honest when it *can't* capture a copy** — never a false promise.

**Managing a real pile**
- A full **edit** space (your note, the summary, the address, the title) and **delete** with one clear confirmation.
- **Import** your whole existing pile at once — folders become split labels, duplicates skipped, original dates preserved — and **export** everything to a take-anywhere file.
- **Sort** by newest / oldest / title, with the date shown quietly.
- **Bulk actions** via a deliberate Select mode: add/remove a label, flag/clear read-later, or delete a batch — "select all" respects your current filter.

**Edge behaviours confirmed:** empty states, non-links refused kindly, background link-rot checks, copies frozen at save-time, dates that age from "just now" to a real date.
